pieces.content:
You belong to the internet or at least an excess of you is handed over. In return, you're given a coat which when on takes up a convex drape. Ok, I imagine you put on the coat, a kind of technical clay to limit your around receptivity. It is blue on the outside and goes together with a yellow inner.

The coat at first goes over your head. You’re a small car through a bored tunnel. The hairs on your arms have nowhere to stand up to cold or a fright. You have a garment sitting on top of you. This entitles an impossible alertness in signal and sense. Yet it’s brief. The clay of the coat itches and vexes. You flop in a loss.

You are soft enough and in a complicated-enough scenario now to meet others, forget their names, dodge their eyes.
pieces.readme: A redesign of a garment I since can't find which you wear to see only the computer monitor—now including both the TuTa and Werther's coat.
pieces.title: Wear coating

pieces.content:
HPE ProLiant DL380’s nostrils dilated as it assiduously surveyed and switched packets. It couldn’t help it. It was about to die; it had better make this count. Capable, though more liant than lion, it had already died many thousands of times since 0000 UTC. It could also slide like a trundle bed.

A signal ran through its not-unhappiness: a request had fluttered their eyelids, the hewn form of which mirrored the short bolts that held up all HPE ProLiant DL380s by their sides arthritically. A look was between us. The nature of the thing was not to ask for anything, instead treating suddenness as immanence.

The look of the request arrived with a crush at the server’s outermost and thick service layer, produced from a pathology of convention and availability. The payload of your eyes is a English-language question about how much effort I exert when I sleep. Something like this doesn’t require parsing, only matching, realised the HPE.
pieces.readme: Old equipment doesn't actually die. It is decommissioned, i.e., has its trust taken away.
pieces.title: Something asking
